messages.author: 9b28b631db3b0ea2
messages.subject: Multilevel beta-binomial
parts:
Hi

I hope this is an ok forum to get feedback on a model I'm working on. The model is included below and it seems to work and compile. But I'm new to heirarchical modeling, and I'd like to get feed back on whether this is reasonable or whether there is a different approach that you'd recommend instead. I'll give a bit of background

I have dataset where we count the total number a certain kind of cell in a specimen (n) and then count a specific sub-type within that total (x). I consider x as a binomial random variable with an unknown proportion, theta. We take these measurements on groups of individuals that have been randomized to one of several treatment groups at baseline prior to treatment and over time after treatment. We also have historical data on the proportion of these cell types over time within and between untreated subjects. 
The STAN model is shown below. theta is true, unknown mean proportion in the untreated population. tau_b is a precision parameter governing the between subject variability around theta. It is gamma distributed and we usually have some information on this -- i.e. not intended to be non-informative. theta_j is the unknown true mean for the jth subject.  At time i, the true sample level mean for subject j will be theta_ij and it fluctuates around theta_j according to a beta distribution with precision parameter tau_w. tau_w is also given an informative or weakly informative gamma prior. Theta_ij is also influence by a set of fixed parameters that I want to make inference on. Specifically, is there a treatment effect (at any dose level) on the proportion of this sub-type of cell. 

Some features of the model that I think I like, are that the baseline samples do not have special importance. They are simply a realization of a beta distributed variable like every other time point. Also, the treatment effect happens at the subject level, theta_j, rather than the global mean, theta. The result is a larger effect for subjects with proportions near 50%, which does seem to capture some aspects of the data we observe. 
I have not applied this prospectively on real data. On data that I've simulated (which complies completely with my assumed distributions -- not realistic), the model seems to work far better than previous linear baseline adjusted models of log transformed data, which I have tried. In fact it works so well, that I suspect I'm not making correct inference here. 

Say X is the design matrix built based on post dose visits including an interaction between dose and visit. Dose groups are reference encoded (placebo = 0s), so other parameters are relative to that. Visits are encoded so they sum to 0 (i.e. the last visit is the -sum(other visits). So for two dose groups and three visits the design matrix is:

Visit  Dose  col1(visit), col2(dose), col3(interaction)
V2     D0      1               0                  0
V2     D1      1               1                  1
V3     D0     -1               0                  0
V3     D1     -1               1                 -1
PRE  any     0               0                  0

I calculate posterior group means from a linear combination of the sampled u's and theta's. inv_logit( L*u + logit(theta) ) and make inferences based on credible intervals. I have also examined the same linear combinations of u to make inference. 

Few specific questions:
  • Is this legit? 
  • How can I ask whether any of the treated groups differ from placebo (comparing lp__ from a model without u?)?
  • I've seen beta-binomial before, but the examples were too simple. Is my model still considered a beta-binomial, or is it beta-beta-beta-binomial??

Sorry this was so long. Thanks for any input. 




model {
   vector[N] theta_i;                        
   
   theta ~ beta(theta_0[1],theta_0[2]);      
   tau_b ~ gamma(gamma_b[1], 1/gamma_b[2] );


   tau_w  ~ gamma( gamma_w[1], 1/gamma_w[2] );
   theta_j ~ beta( tau_b*theta, tau_b*(1-theta) );      


   u ~ normal( u_0, se_0 );         // prior for "fixed" coefficients
   
   for (i in 1:N) {
        theta_i[i] <- inv_logit( X[i]*u + logit(theta_j[grp_i[i]]) );
        }


    theta_ij ~ beta( theta_i*tau_w, (1-theta_i)*tau_w );
    x ~ binomial( n,theta_ij );


 }


Results compared to mixed effects baseline adjusted linear model. blue '+' is the truth. I've done many simulations and the coverage of the credible intervals is good and the credible intervals are smaller than those from a mixed model.

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Multilevel beta-binomial
parts:
Sorry --- we're getting bogged down with all the people sending us
long and involved models these days. So posts that don't lead
with a specific question tend to get ignored.

I'll give your questions a shot.

1. Yes, it's kosher to transform the variables you sample. That's
just a new random variable defined as a function of the old ones and
the posterior's legit. You should do this in Stan's generated quantities
so you can monitor convergence.

2. Didn't get the context about comparing. But in general, you want
to do a posterior event probability along the lines of Pr[theta[1] > theta[2]].
In Stan, that just means assigning an int value to 1 if the property holds
and 0 otherwise and looking at the posterior mean.

3. Beta-binomial is a distribution that marginalizes the binomial parameter
out of a compound beta-binomial:

p(y, theta | a, b) = beta(theta | a, b) * binomial(y | N, theta)

and then marginalizing out theta to get

BetaBinom(y | a, b)

= INTEGRAL_0^1 beta(theta | a, b) * binomial(y | N, theta) d.theta

- Bob
